title: Endocrine Disorders: Thyroid and Diabetes in Pregnancy

units.title: Maternal Thyroid Physiology & Hypothyroidism
units.guide: Gestational hCG cross-reacts with TSH receptors during the first trimester, causing a physiological dip in TSH and transient thyrotoxicosis. Maternal overt hypothyroidism (TSH >=2.5 in T1, >=3.0 in T2/T3) is managed with levothyroxine, requiring a 30-50% dose escalation during pregnancy to support fetal neurocognitive development.

units.title: Gestational Hyperthyroidism & Antithyroid Protocols
units.guide: Graves' disease is the leading cause of hyperthyroidism in pregnancy. Propylthiouracil (PTU) is preferred during first-trimester organogenesis to avoid methimazole-induced embryopathy (aplasia cutis, choanal atresia), with a planned transition to methimazole in the second trimester to avoid maternal PTU hepatotoxicity.

units.title: Gestational Diabetes Mellitus: Etiology & Screening
units.guide: Placental diabetogenic hormones—predominantly Human Placental Lactogen (hPL), cortisol, and progesterone—peak in the late second trimester, inducing physiological peripheral insulin resistance. Under DIPSI guidelines, a non-fasting single-step 75g oral glucose challenge with a 2-hour plasma glucose >=140 mg/dL establishes the diagnosis of GDM.

units.title: White's Classification, Risk Factors & Glycemic Targets
units.guide: Priscilla White's classification stratifies pregnancy diabetes: Class A1 (diet-controlled GDM), Class A2 (medication-requiring GDM), and Classes B through H denoting vascular complications. Recommended glycemic targets are fasting glucose <95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial <140 mg/dL, 2-hour postprandial <120 mg/dL, and HbA1c <6.0-6.5%.

units.title: Medical Nutrition Therapy & Insulin Pharmacotherapy
units.guide: Initial management of GDM begins with medical nutrition therapy for up to 2 weeks. If glycemic goals are unmet, subcutaneous insulin represents the gold standard pharmacotherapy because it does not cross the placenta; rapid-acting analogs (lispro, aspart) and basal detemir or NPH provide safe and predictable control.

units.title: Diabetic Embryopathy & Structural Malformations
units.guide: First-trimester maternal hyperglycemia induces oxidative stress leading to diabetic embryopathy. Sacral agenesis (caudal regression syndrome) is the most specific anomaly associated with pregestational diabetes (200-400x increased risk), while ventricular septal defect (VSD) is the most common congenital heart anomaly.

units.title: Fetal Macrosomia, Polyhydramnios & Neonatal Metabolism
units.guide: According to the Pedersen hypothesis, maternal hyperglycemia produces fetal hyperinsulinism, driving accelerated somatic growth (macrosomia with shoulder-head disproportion), asymmetric septal cardiac hypertrophy, and polyhydramnios. Postnatal cord clamping abruptly cuts off maternal glucose, precipitating acute neonatal hypoglycemia within the first 1-2 hours of life.

units.title: Intrapartum Glycemic Control, Delivery Timing & Postpartum Follow-Up
units.guide: Intrapartum glucose is maintained between 80 and 110 mg/dL via insulin-dextrose infusions to prevent rebound neonatal hypoglycemia. Elective Caesarean delivery is advised if estimated fetal weight exceeds 4.5 kg to avoid shoulder dystocia. Maternal insulin requirements plummet immediately post-placental delivery, and a 75g OGTT is scheduled at 6-12 weeks postpartum.

questions.q: Why does maternal serum Thyroid-Stimulating Hormone (TSH) exhibit a physiological decline during the late first trimester of normal pregnancy?
opts: Peak levels of hCG share an identical alpha-subunit with TSH and cross-stimulate thyroid TSH receptors, transiently suppressing pituitary TSH
Maternal thyroid gland undergoes extensive physiological atrophy
Placental lactogen destroys maternal pituitary thyrotrophs
Renal excretion of TSH increases ten-fold
questions.exp: The alpha subunit of hCG is structurally homologous to TSH; high T1 hCG stimulates the thyroid, mildly suppressing pituitary TSH. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the recommended upper normal cutoff for maternal serum TSH in the first trimester versus the second and third trimesters of pregnancy?
opts: < 2.5 mIU/L in the first trimester; < 3.0 mIU/L in the second and third trimesters
questions.exp: Gestational TSH target thresholds: < 2.5 mIU/L in T1 and < 3.0 mIU/L in T2 and T3. (Book p375)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with pre-existing hypothyroidism on levothyroxine confirms conception. How should her levothyroxine replacement dosage be adjusted?
opts: Increase the pre-pregnancy levothyroxine dose by approximately 30% to 50% immediately upon pregnancy confirmation
Decrease the levothyroxine dose by 50% to prevent fetal thyrotoxicosis
Discontinue levothyroxine until after the first trimester
Maintain the exact same dose without repeat testing
questions.exp: Estrogen increases thyroid-binding globulin and placental deiodinase-3 degrades T4, necessitating a 30-50% dose increase upon conception. (Book p375)

questions.q: Untreated maternal overt hypothyroidism during the first half of pregnancy is strongly associated with which serious fetal complication?
opts: Permanent neurocognitive impairment, low IQ, and congenital cretinism
questions.exp: The fetal thyroid only functions after 12-14 weeks; maternal T4 is vital for early fetal cerebral development, and deficiency causes neurocognitive deficits. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the most frequent autoimmune etiology of overt hypothyroidism in pregnant women living in non-iodine-deficient geographic areas?
opts: Hashimoto thyroiditis (chronic autoimmune thyroiditis with anti-TPO antibodies)
questions.exp: Hashimoto's thyroiditis (marked by anti-thyroid peroxidase and anti-thyroglobulin antibodies) is the leading cause of gestational hypothyroidism. (Book p375)

questions.q: What is the antithyroid drug of choice during the FIRST TRIMESTER of pregnancy for managing Graves' disease?
opts: Propylthiouracil (PTU), to minimize the risk of methimazole-associated embryopathy
Methimazole, because it never crosses the placenta
questions.exp: PTU is preferred in the 1st trimester because methimazole causes congenital malformations like aplasia cutis and choanal atresia. (Book p375)

questions.q: Why is the patient transitioned from Propylthiouracil (PTU) to Methimazole starting in the SECOND TRIMESTER?
opts: To protect the mother against severe PTU-induced fulminant hepatic necrosis, while organogenesis is complete
Because PTU stops functioning after 14 weeks
Because methimazole is cheaper in late pregnancy
questions.exp: PTU carries an FDA black-box warning for lethal maternal hepatotoxicity; once organogenesis concludes, switching to methimazole is safer. (Book p375)

questions.q: Why is Radioactive Iodine (I-131) therapy ABSOLUTELY CONTRAINDICATED throughout pregnancy?
opts: It readily crosses the placenta and permanently ablates the fetal thyroid gland, causing severe congenital hypothyroidism
It triggers immediate uterine hyperstimulation and rupture
questions.exp: I-131 crosses the placenta, is avidly taken up by the fetal thyroid after 10-12 weeks, and destroys it, causing severe cretinism. (Book p375)

questions.q: A pregnant woman with Graves' disease presents with high fever, delirium, tachycardia (>140 bpm), and jaundice. What acute life-threatening endocrine emergency is this, and what is the initial drug of choice?
opts: Thyroid storm; managed with intravenous PTU, Lugol's iodine, beta-blockers, and hydrocortisone
questions.exp: Thyroid storm carries high maternal/fetal mortality; therapy combines high-dose PTU (blocks T4 synthesis/peripheral T3 conversion), iodine, steroids, and propranolol. (Book p375)

questions.q: Which placental hormone is primarily responsible for the progressive peripheral maternal insulin resistance that develops during the second half of pregnancy?
opts: Human Placental Lactogen (hPL / Human Chorionic Somatomammotropin)
questions.exp: Human placental lactogen (hPL), along with cortisol, progesterone, and TNF-alpha, acts as a potent anti-insulin hormone peaking at 24-28 weeks. (Book p376)

questions.q: According to the Diabetes in Pregnancy Study Group India (DIPSI) guidelines, how is screening and diagnosis for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) performed?
opts: Single-step non-fasting oral administration of 75 g of glucose; plasma glucose >= 140 mg/dL at 2 hours is diagnostic of GDM
Two-step 100 g fasting test requiring 4 blood samples
Random fasting capillary blood glucose alone
questions.exp: DIPSI criteria: single-step non-fasting 75g glucose challenge given irrespective of last meal; 2-hour venous plasma glucose >= 140 mg/dL diagnoses GDM. (Book p377)

questions.q: Under IADPSG (International Association of Diabetes and Pregnancy Study Groups) criteria, GDM is diagnosed if any ONE value meets or exceeds which 75g OGTT cutoffs?
questions.exp: IADPSG fasting >=92 mg/dL, 1-hour >=180 mg/dL, or 2-hour >=153 mg/dL after 75g glucose load; meeting any single threshold confirms GDM. (Book p377)

questions.q: At what gestational age is universal screening for Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) routinely recommended for pregnant women without prior risk factors?
questions.exp: Universal GDM testing is scheduled between 24 and 28 weeks, when placental anti-insulin hormone secretion surges. (Book p378)

questions.q: If a pregnant woman possesses high-risk features for diabetes (e.g., prior GDM, BMI >30, polycystic ovarian syndrome, family history), when should she be screened?
opts: At the very first antenatal booking visit, repeating at 24-28 weeks if initially negative
questions.exp: High-risk women should undergo early testing at the initial booking visit to detect undiagnosed pre-existing diabetes; if negative, retest at 24-28w. (Book p378)

questions.q: In Priscilla White's classification of diabetes in pregnancy, what distinguishes Class A1 from Class A2 gestational diabetes?
opts: Class A1 is diet-controlled GDM; Class A2 requires pharmacological therapy (insulin or oral hypoglycemics)
Class A1 develops before pregnancy; Class A2 develops during pregnancy
Class A1 has diabetic nephropathy; Class A2 has retinopathy
Class A1 is treated with dialysis
questions.exp: Class A1 represents GDM well-controlled with medical nutrition therapy alone; Class A2 represents GDM requiring medications. (Book p378)

questions.q: In White's classification, which subclass indicates diabetes complicated by proliferative diabetic retinopathy?
questions.exp: Class R denotes diabetic retinopathy, Class F denotes nephropathy (proteinuria >500 mg/d), and Class H denotes coronary artery disease. (Book p378)

questions.q: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) in pregnant women is a medical emergency that differs from the non-pregnant state because it:
opts: Can develop rapidly at significantly lower, near-normal blood glucose levels (euglycemic DKA with glucose < 200 mg/dL)
Is caused by excess insulin administration
questions.exp: Gestational DKA occurs at lower glucose levels (<200 mg/dL) due to respiratory alkalosis and rapid ketogenesis, carrying a 20-30% fetal mortality. (Book p379)

questions.q: What are the recommended maternal home blood glucose monitoring targets for a woman with gestational diabetes?
opts: Fasting < 95 mg/dL; 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL; 2-hour postprandial < 120 mg/dL
questions.exp: ACOG/ADA gestational targets: fasting < 95 mg/dL, 1-hour postprandial < 140 mg/dL, and 2-hour postprandial < 120 mg/dL. (Book p381)

questions.q: What target Glycated Hemoglobin (HbA1c) level is recommended during pregnancy to minimize risks of congenital malformations and fetal macrosomia?
questions.exp: An HbA1c < 6.0-6.5% achieves optimal perinatal outcomes without inducing maternal hypoglycemic episodes. (Book p382)

questions.q: When Gestational Diabetes Mellitus is newly diagnosed, what is the initial management step before starting pharmacological therapy?
opts: Medical Nutrition Therapy (MNT) and moderate exercise for 1 to 2 weeks
Immediate initiation of high-dose intravenous insulin
questions.exp: First-line management is MNT (30 kcal/kg/day, balanced complex carbohydrates) with lifestyle modification for up to 2 weeks. (Book p381)

questions.q: Why is a complex carbohydrate bedtime snack recommended for pregnant women with diabetes managed on insulin?
opts: To prevent nocturnal hypoglycemia and subsequent rebound morning ketosis / Somogyi effect
questions.exp: A bedtime protein-carbohydrate snack prevents overnight fasting hypoglycemia and starvation ketonuria during the long sleeping interval. (Book p383)

questions.q: What is the pharmacological DRUG OF CHOICE for managing gestational diabetes when medical nutrition therapy fails to meet glycemic targets?
opts: Subcutaneous Insulin (does not cross the placenta)
questions.exp: Insulin is the gold standard because it effectively normalizes maternal blood glucose without crossing the placental syncytiotrophoblast. (Book p384)

questions.q: Which rapid-acting insulin analogs are safe and approved for mealtime glucose control during pregnancy?
questions.exp: Insulin lispro and aspart are Category B rapid-acting analogs that control postprandial spikes safely in pregnancy. (Book p384)

questions.q: If an oral hypoglycemic agent is chosen for a patient with GDM who refuses insulin injections, which medication is most commonly prescribed?
opts: Metformin (biguanide that crosses the placenta without adverse teratogenicity)
questions.exp: Metformin crosses the placenta but has an established safety profile, making it the most accepted oral alternative to insulin. (Book p385)

questions.q: What is the single MOST SPECIFIC congenital malformation associated with pre-existing maternal pregestational diabetes mellitus?
opts: Sacral agenesis / Caudal regression syndrome (200- to 400-fold increased risk)
questions.exp: Sacral agenesis (caudal regression syndrome) is rare in the general population but exhibits a 200-400x increased incidence in maternal diabetes. (Book p386)

questions.q: What is the most COMMON congenital cardiovascular malformation identified in infants of diabetic mothers?
questions.exp: VSD and transposition of the great arteries (TGA) are the most common cardiac structural malformations in maternal diabetes. (Book p386)

questions.q: Why does maternal gestational diabetes mellitus diagnosed in the late second trimester (at 26 weeks) NOT cause major structural organ malformations like neural tube or cardiac defects?
opts: Because fetal organogenesis is completed by the end of the 8th to 10th week after fertilization
Because fetal kidneys destroy maternal glucose
Because GDM prevents all placental transfer
Because high estrogen protects embryonic organs
questions.exp: Organogenesis occurs in the first trimester (weeks 3-8 post-fertilization); GDM develops late and causes fetal overgrowth, not organ dysgenesis. (Book p387)

questions.q: What transient cardiac structural abnormality occurs in up to 30% of infants of diabetic mothers due to fetal hyperinsulinism?
opts: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy (hypertrophic cardiomyopathy that regresses postpartum)
questions.exp: Fetal hyperinsulinism stimulates glycogen and fat deposition in the interventricular septum, producing transient asymmetric septal hypertrophy. (Book p387)

questions.q: What is the lifetime risk of developing Type 2 diabetes mellitus in offspring born to mothers with gestational diabetes?
opts: Significantly elevated (approximately 1% to 3% in childhood/adolescence, rising to up to 20-40% in adult life)
Reduced due to acquired immune tolerance
questions.exp: Intrauterine exposure to hyperglycemia programmes fetal adiposity and beta-cell dysfunction, raising long-term risk of obesity and Type 2 diabetes. (Book p388)

questions.q: According to the Pedersen hypothesis, what sequence of pathophysiological events explains fetal macrosomia in diabetic pregnancies?
opts: Maternal hyperglycemia leads to fetal hyperglycemia, which triggers fetal pancreatic beta-cell hyperplasia and hyperinsulinism
Excess maternal insulin crosses the placenta and stimulates fetal bone elongation
Fetal somatostatin increases fetal growth hormone
questions.exp: Glucose freely crosses the placenta while maternal insulin does not; fetal hyperglycemia stimulates fetal insulin, which acts as a growth hormone. (Book p387)

questions.q: Fetal macrosomia in diabetic mothers is asymmetrical, featuring excessive deposition of fat over the shoulders and trunk. This disproportion significantly predisposes to:
questions.exp: Hyperinsulinism produces disproportionate shoulder and trunk fat deposition (increased shoulder-to-head ratio), predisposing to shoulder dystocia. (Book p387)

questions.q: Why is polyhydramnios frequently observed in pregnant women with poorly controlled gestational diabetes?
opts: Fetal hyperglycemia induces osmotic diuresis, causing marked fetal polyuria into the amniotic cavity
Fetal esophageal atresia prevents fluid swallowing
Maternal amniotic fluid transudation from high blood pressure
Placental membrane tears leaking maternal serum
questions.exp: Fetal hyperglycemia causes osmotic diuresis; increased fetal micturition elevates amniotic fluid volume, producing polyhydramnios. (Book p387)

questions.q: Why do neonates of diabetic mothers rapidly develop severe hypoglycemia within the first 1 to 2 hours following birth?
opts: Umbilical cord clamping abruptly cuts off high maternal glucose supply, while autonomous fetal hyperinsulinism persists
The neonate fails to produce glucagon permanently
The neonate's liver cannot store glycogen
Insulin is degraded in the neonatal circulation
questions.exp: Cord severance halts maternal glucose delivery, but the infant's hypertrophied beta cells continue hypersecreting insulin, dropping blood sugar. (Book p388)

questions.q: Why are neonates of diabetic mothers at increased risk of Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) even when delivered near term?
opts: High fetal insulin levels antagonize cortisol, inhibiting the synthesis of pulmonary surfactant (specifically phosphatidylglycerol)
Fetal lungs fill with amniotic glucose
Diabetic neonates lack type I pneumocytes
Fetal insulin destroys the thoracic cage
questions.exp: Hyperinsulinism inhibits surfactant synthesis in alveolar type II pneumocytes, delaying biochemical lung maturation and predisposing to RDS. (Book p388)

questions.q: What is the target maternal blood glucose range maintained during active labor in a diabetic patient using intravenous insulin-dextrose infusion?
questions.exp: Strict intrapartum control between 80 and 110 mg/dL prevents acute intrapartum fetal acidemia and immediate post-delivery neonatal hypoglycemia. (Book p385)

questions.q: Immediately following delivery of the placenta, how does maternal insulin requirement change in a woman with pregestational Type 1 diabetes?
opts: Insulin requirements plummet precipitously (often decreasing by >= 50% compared to third-trimester doses)
questions.exp: Placental expulsion removes all circulating anti-insulin hormones (hPL, progesterone, cortisol), rapidly restoring maternal insulin sensitivity. (Book p385)

questions.q: What estimated fetal weight cutoff on prenatal ultrasound justifies elective Caesarean section in a diabetic mother to prevent catastrophic brachial plexus injury?
opts: Estimated fetal weight >= 4.5 kg (or >= 4000 g with clinical disproportion)
questions.exp: ACOG recommends offering elective CS when estimated fetal weight is >= 4.5 kg in diabetic mothers to avert shoulder dystocia and Erb's palsy. (Book p389)

questions.q: For a woman diagnosed with Gestational Diabetes Mellitus during pregnancy, when and how should postpartum glycemic re-evaluation be performed?
opts: At 6 to 12 weeks postpartum, using a standard 2-hour 75 g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT)
At 1 week postpartum using a fasting urine dipstick
At 1 year using random blood glucose
No postpartum testing is necessary once baby is delivered
questions.exp: A 75g 2-hour OGTT at 6-12 weeks postpartum is mandatory to identify mothers who have transitioned to impaired glucose tolerance or overt diabetes. (Book p390)
